newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl lashes out at his labour minister Bluem.
newsitem.headline: Kohl lashes out at his labour minister Bluem.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl criticised Labour Minister Norbert Bluem on Saturday for his public doubts about the government's pension reform plans, but Kohl said he had no intention of firing his long-time ally.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of the Chrisitian Democrats (CDU), called on the party to end the "poisonous discussion" on tax and pension reform.
"We are destroying ourselves with this debate," Schaeuble told the Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung.
Kohl was quoted in an interview in the newsweekly magazine Focus saying recent remarks from Bluem, like Kohl a member of the Christian Democrats (CDU), were "completely unacceptable."
Kohl added in the interview to be published on Monday: "We are good friends so we should also be able to have a dispute...Bluem is in the cabinet and I have absolutely no intention of changing that."

The chancellor's remarks caused an immediate stir because Bluem's departure would expose an ominous and potentially lethal rift for Kohl's government, now in its 14th year in power and dogged by repeated turbulence in recent months.
Bluem has been a highly loyal ally to Kohl and the only minister to have served in every Kohl government since 1982.
Bluem has been seething in private for weeks over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to raise taxes on pensions and over other matters linked to the sweeping tax reform proposals.
But Bluem's complaints went public on Friday.

"I will not hide my dispute with the Chancellor," Bluem said in a debate in parliament and the minister was quoted in the Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper saying: "Kohl is always telling me -- 'Don't worry, we will help you'. But I can't rely on that any more."
Kohl appeared stunned by the comment: "Did he really say that?" Kohl said in the Focus interview.
Bluem unveiled plans last week to cut old-age pensions, raise contributions and launch a tax-financed "family fund" to keep the compulsory pensions scheme going in the 21st century.
